AUTHNOTT.name: Permits authorized, not started
AUTHNOTT.read: A swelling backlog means builders hold entitlements and are choosing not to break ground.
AUTHNOTT.example: For example: a builder pulls permits for a 200-home phase but only breaks ground on 140 this quarter. The other 60 sit in this backlog until they either start construction or the permit expires.
AUTHNOTT.title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Authorized but Not Started: Total Units

PERMIT.name: Building permits, total
PERMIT.read: The front of the construction pipeline. Turns before starts by one to two quarters.
PERMIT.example: For example: a jump here in March typically shows up as more dirt turning in housing starts by around May or June.
PERMIT.title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Authorized in Permit-Issuing Places: Total Units

PERMIT1.name: Single-family permits
PERMIT1.read: Cleaner than the total, which multifamily swings distort.
PERMIT1.example: For example: one large apartment complex getting a single permit for 300 units can swing the total-permits number sharply in a month; this series strips that out.
PERMIT1.title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Authorized in Permit-Issuing Places: Single-Family Units

HOUST1F.name: Single-family housing starts
HOUST1F.read: Where permits become dirt. Compare against permits to see the conversion rate.
HOUST1F.example: For example: if permits ran at 100,000 last month but starts only hit 80,000, roughly 20,000 homes are sitting between paperwork and groundbreaking.
HOUST1F.title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Started: Single-Family Units

HOUST.name: Housing starts, total
HOUST.read: Total starts including multifamily, which swings hard on a few large projects.
HOUST.example: For example: one large 400-unit apartment tower breaking ground can move this number more than a hundred small single-family starts combined.
HOUST.title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Started: Total Units

MORTGAGE30US.name: 30-year fixed mortgage rate
MORTGAGE30US.read: The affordability lever. Direction and speed matter more than the level.
MORTGAGE30US.example: For example: on a $400,000 loan, moving from 6.5% to 7.0% adds roughly $130 to the monthly payment, enough to price some buyers out entirely.
MORTGAGE30US.title: 30-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States

UMCSENT.name: Consumer sentiment
UMCSENT.read: Headline sentiment is a weak housing signal on its own, but it turns early.
UMCSENT.example: For example: sentiment can drop sharply after a bad headline even while people keep buying homes at the same pace, which is why it counts as a weak signal on its own.
UMCSENT.title: University of Michigan: Consumer Sentiment

TDSP.name: Household debt service ratio
TDSP.read: How stretched household budgets already are before a payment shock.
TDSP.example: For example: when this ratio is already elevated, a small rise in rates or a job loss leaves far less room to absorb before a household falls behind on payments.
TDSP.title: Household Debt Service Payments as a Percent of Disposable Personal Income

T10Y2Y.name: 2s10s curve
T10Y2Y.read: 10-year minus 2-year. Below zero is an inversion, which has led recessions by roughly a year. Steepening back above zero is the signal, not the inversion itself.
T10Y2Y.example: For example: in 2022 this curve went negative for the first time in years, correctly flagging elevated recession risk roughly a year ahead of when growth actually slowed.
T10Y2Y.title: 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity

DGS2.name: 2-year Treasury
DGS2.read: Tracks where the market thinks policy is going over the next two years.
DGS2.example: For example: this yield tends to rise when the market expects the Fed to keep raising rates, and fall once cuts are expected.
DGS2.title: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 2-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis

DGS10.name: 10-year Treasury
DGS10.read: The base the 30-year mortgage prices off. Watch the gap between the two.
DGS10.example: For example: the 30-year mortgage rate usually runs about 1.5 to 2.5 points above this yield; a mortgage rate far outside that range signals something else, like spread widening, is going on.
DGS10.title: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 10-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis

DGS30.name: 30-year Treasury
DGS30.read: The long end of the curve. Matters more for the long-term mortgage that eventually replaces a construction loan than for the construction loan itself.
DGS30.example: For example: a builder using construction-to-permanent financing cares more about where this yield sits at the time of the permanent take-out loan than at groundbreaking.
DGS30.title: Market Yield on U.S. Treasury Securities at 30-Year Constant Maturity, Quoted on an Investment Basis

SOFR.name: SOFR, overnight
SOFR.read: The overnight secured rate that replaced LIBOR in 2023. The floor under floating construction debt.
SOFR.example: For example: a construction loan priced at "SOFR plus 250bp" moves dollar-for-dollar with this rate every time it resets.
SOFR.title: Secured Overnight Financing Rate

SOFR30DAYAVG.name: SOFR 30-day average
SOFR30DAYAVG.read: Backward-looking compounded average from the New York Fed. The closest free public stand-in for 1-month Term SOFR, which is licensed and not on FRED.
SOFR30DAYAVG.example: For example: a loan that resets monthly and references 1-month Term SOFR will track very close to this series, since it is the closest free public substitute.
SOFR30DAYAVG.title: 30-Day Average SOFR

SOFR90DAYAVG.name: SOFR 90-day average
SOFR90DAYAVG.read: The quarterly-reset equivalent. Use this one if your loan's rate resets every quarter rather than monthly.
SOFR90DAYAVG.example: For example: a facility that resets every quarter will track this series more closely than the overnight or 30-day figures.
SOFR90DAYAVG.title: 90-Day Average SOFR

DPRIME.name: Bank prime loan rate
DPRIME.read: What smaller land and construction loans actually price off. Moves in lockstep with the fed funds rate, historically about 300bp above it.
DPRIME.example: For example: a small local construction loan quoted at "prime plus 1%" moves in direct lockstep with this number.
DPRIME.title: Bank Prime Loan Rate

FEDFUNDS.name: Federal funds rate
FEDFUNDS.read: The policy rate. Housing responds to the long end, but this sets the tone.
FEDFUNDS.example: For example: a quarter-point Fed cut here does not guarantee the 30-year mortgage rate moves at all in the short run, since mortgage pricing follows the 10-year Treasury more closely.
FEDFUNDS.title: Federal Funds Effective Rate

MORTGAGE15US.name: 15-year fixed mortgage
MORTGAGE15US.read: The gap to the 30-year shows how much of the curve borrowers are paying for.
MORTGAGE15US.example: For example: a 15-year loan often carries a rate half a point or more below the 30-year on the same day, reflecting the shorter payoff period.
MORTGAGE15US.title: 15-Year Fixed Rate Mortgage Average in the United States

BAMLC0A4CBBB.name: BBB corporate spread
BAMLC0A4CBBB.read: Investment-grade credit stress. When this widens, it gets more expensive for builders to draw on their revolving credit lines, tightening their cash position before it ever shows up in a housing number.
BAMLC0A4CBBB.example: For example: if this widens by 50bp, a builder's next bond issuance or credit facility renewal likely gets priced meaningfully more expensively, even if Treasury yields have not moved at all.
BAMLC0A4CBBB.title: ICE BofA BBB US Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread

BAMLH0A0HYM2.name: High yield spread
BAMLH0A0HYM2.read: The risk appetite gauge. Blows out first when credit turns.
BAMLH0A0HYM2.example: For example: this spread often jumps well before equity markets sell off, since credit investors tend to reprice risk first.
BAMLH0A0HYM2.title: ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread

HSN1F.name: New home sales
HSN1F.read: Recorded at contract signing, so slightly ahead of existing sales.
HSN1F.example: For example: a buyer signing a contract on a to-be-built home in March counts here immediately, even though the sale will not close for months.
HSN1F.title: New One Family Houses Sold: United States

MSACSR.name: Months supply, new homes
MSACSR.read: How many months it would take to sell every new home currently on the market at the current sales pace. A rising number means inventory is building up faster than it is selling; above roughly six months has historically preceded builders cutting prices to move it.
MSACSR.example: For example: at 10,000 homes for sale and 1,500 selling per month, that is roughly 6.7 months of supply, a level that has historically preceded builders cutting prices.
MSACSR.title: Monthly Supply of New Houses in the United States

EXHOSLUSM495S.name: Existing home sales
EXHOSLUSM495S.read: Previously owned homes changing hands, the resale market, as opposed to new construction. Counted at closing, so a home that went under contract in one month often does not show up here until the next, a month or two after the buyer actually decided.
EXHOSLUSM495S.example: For example: a home that goes under contract in March typically does not count here until the sale closes in April or May.
EXHOSLUSM495S.title: Existing Home Sales

COMPUTSA.name: Housing completions
COMPUTSA.read: Supply arriving now from starts twelve to eighteen months ago.
COMPUTSA.example: For example: a wave of apartment buildings that broke ground in a hot construction year will show up as completions here roughly twelve to eighteen months later, arriving on the market around the same time.
COMPUTSA.title: New Privately-Owned Housing Units Completed: Total Units

MSPUS.name: Median sales price, US homes
MSPUS.read: Mix-sensitive. A falling median can mean cheaper homes selling, not falling values.
MSPUS.example: For example: if builders shift toward more starter homes and fewer luxury homes, this median can fall even while every single home sells for more than it did last year.
MSPUS.title: Median Sales Price of New Houses Sold for the United States

CSUSHPINSA.name: Case-Shiller national
CSUSHPINSA.read: An index of home prices nationally, tracking the same houses as they resell over time rather than a raw median of whatever happened to sell. Built from a three-month moving average and published two months late, so it confirms a price turn well after it already happened.
CSUSHPINSA.example: For example: because this uses a three-month moving average reported two months late, a price turn that already happened in July might not clearly show up here until October.
CSUSHPINSA.title: S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index
CSUSHPINSA.release_name: S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices

WPUSI012011.name: Construction materials PPI
WPUSI012011.read: Reaches a builder's cost projections before it reaches their completed, as-built cost.
WPUSI012011.example: For example: a spike in lumber or steel prices here typically shows up in a builder's cost projections before it ever appears in their actual completed-home costs.
WPUSI012011.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Special Indexes: Construction Materials

JTS2300JOL.name: Construction job openings
JTS2300JOL.read: Hiring intent turns before payrolls. Better labor read than employment level.
JTS2300JOL.example: For example: a builder posting more openings for framers and electricians this month is signaling planned activity before a single new hire shows up on payroll.
JTS2300JOL.title: Job Openings: Construction
JTS2300JOL.release_name: Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey

USCONS.name: Construction employment
USCONS.read: How many people are actually on construction payrolls, as opposed to job openings, which measures hiring intent. Useful mainly as a check on whether posted openings are actually turning into hires.
USCONS.example: For example: this confirms whether the hiring intent shown by job openings actually turned into people getting hired.
USCONS.title: All Employees, Construction

PRRESCONS.name: Residential construction spend
PRRESCONS.read: The dollar value of construction work actually completed in the period, not contracts signed or work planned, so it reflects work already underway.
PRRESCONS.example: For example: this counts the dollar value of a foundation actually poured this month, not the total contract value of a home that will take a year to build.
PRRESCONS.title: Total Private Construction Spending: Residential in the United States

DRSFRMACBS.name: SF mortgage delinquency
DRSFRMACBS.read: Lags badly but confirms turns. Watch the rate of change, not the level.
DRSFRMACBS.example: For example: this rate was still near normal levels well after the 2008 housing bust had already begun, since missed payments take months to show up as a formally delinquent loan.
DRSFRMACBS.title: Delinquency Rate on Single-Family Residential Mortgages, Booked in Domestic Offices, All Commercial Banks
DRSFRMACBS.release_name: Charge-Off and Delinquency Rates on Loans and Leases at Commercial Banks

DRCRELEXFACBS.name: CRE loan delinquency
DRCRELEXFACBS.read: Banks classify loans on income-producing properties like apartment buildings, offices, and retail centers as commercial real estate, separate from a single-family home mortgage. Apartment buildings are the sub-segment to watch here: many broke ground in the same building boom and are finishing construction around the same time, so a wave of new units ends up competing for renters in the same local markets at once.
DRCRELEXFACBS.example: For example: a 300-unit apartment building takes out a commercial loan to get built, then opens into a neighborhood where several similar buildings just finished too. All of them are chasing the same renters, so it fills more slowly than planned, rents come under pressure to attract tenants, and the building's income falls short of what its loan payment assumed.
DRCRELEXFACBS.title: Delinquency Rate on Commercial Real Estate Loans (Excluding Farmland), Booked in Domestic Offices, All Commercial Banks
DRCRELEXFACBS.release_name: Charge-Off and Delinquency Rates on Loans and Leases at Commercial Banks

CABPPRIV.name: California permits authorized
CABPPRIV.read: State pipeline. Compare against national permits to see if California is diverging.
CABPPRIV.example: For example: if California's permit count falls while the national number holds steady, that is a sign the state's slowdown is more severe, or starting earlier, than the rest of the country.
CABPPRIV.title: New Private Housing Units Authorized by Building Permits for California
CABPPRIV.release_name: Housing Units Authorized By Building Permits

CASTHPI.name: California house price index
CASTHPI.read: A home price index for California specifically, built from every recorded sale and refinance appraisal the regulator can access, not just a sample. Published quarterly, slower to update than Case-Shiller but consistent over time.
CASTHPI.example: For example: this index is built from repeat sales of the same homes over time, so it tracks value changes more cleanly than a raw median price, which mixes in whatever happened to sell that quarter.
CASTHPI.title: All-Transactions House Price Index for California

LXXRSA.name: Los Angeles Case-Shiller
LXXRSA.read: Your metro, same two-month lag as the national index.
LXXRSA.example: For example: Los Angeles can diverge from the statewide CASTHPI number if the coastal metro is cooling while inland California markets stay hot, or the other way around.
LXXRSA.title: S&P Cotality Case-Shiller CA-Los Angeles Home Price Index
LXXRSA.release_name: S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices

CAUR.name: California unemployment
CAUR.read: Context for how fast homes actually sell. Rising unemployment shrinks the pool of qualified buyers before prices move.
CAUR.example: For example: a local employer announcing layoffs shrinks the pool of people who can qualify for a mortgage in that area, months before it shows up as softer home sales.
CAUR.title: Unemployment Rate in California

DCOILWTICO.name: Crude oil, WTI
DCOILWTICO.read: The US benchmark oil price. Feeds construction costs indirectly, through diesel for equipment and trucking, asphalt for paving, and the plastics and adhesives used throughout a home, more than through any single material directly.
DCOILWTICO.example: For example: a $20 jump in the price of a barrel of oil raises the diesel cost of running excavators and delivery trucks on a job site, and pushes up asphalt prices for driveways and roads, without a single stick of lumber changing price.
DCOILWTICO.title: Crude Oil Prices: West Texas Intermediate (WTI) - Cushing, Oklahoma

WPU081.name: Lumber
WPU081.read: Producer price index for softwood and hardwood lumber. The most volatile major input in home construction: framing lumber prices have swung by more than half within a single year before, driven by mill capacity, tariffs, and wildfire or beetle damage to timber supply.
WPU081.example: For example: lumber prices roughly tripled in a few months during 2021, adding an estimated $20,000 or more to the cost of building a typical new single-family home before falling back just as fast.
WPU081.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Lumber and Wood Products: Lumber

WPU101704.name: Steel, structural
WPU101704.read: Producer price index for hot rolled steel bars, plates, and structural shapes, the form steel takes in a building's frame and rebar rather than sheet steel used in cars or appliances.
WPU101704.example: For example: a builder pricing out a large custom home with steel beam supports gets a materials quote that is only valid for 30 days, because the mill's own price can move meaningfully before the steel is even delivered.
WPU101704.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Metals and Metal Products: Hot Rolled Steel Bars, Plates, and Structural Shapes

WPUSI019011.name: Copper
WPUSI019011.read: Producer price index across copper and copper products. Runs through electrical wiring and plumbing pipe and fittings; a global industrial metal, so it moves with worldwide demand and mine supply more than with US housing activity specifically.
WPUSI019011.example: For example: a spike in global copper prices, driven by demand from data centers or electric vehicles rather than anything happening in US housing, still raises the cost of wiring a new home.
WPUSI019011.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Special Indexes: Copper and Copper Products

WPU1333.name: Ready-mix concrete
WPU1333.read: Producer price index for ready-mix concrete, the slab, footings and flatwork of a house. Moves with cement, aggregate and diesel costs and rarely falls.
WPU1333.example: For example: a slab-on-grade tract home pours roughly 50 to 80 cubic yards of concrete across foundation, driveway and walks, so a few dollars a yard repeats across every lot in a phase.
WPU1333.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Nonmetallic Mineral Products: Ready-Mix Concrete

WPU137.name: Gypsum products (drywall)
WPU137.read: Producer price index for gypsum products, mostly wallboard. A large-volume interior material whose plants run on natural gas.
WPU137.example: For example: a 2,500 square foot house hangs on the order of 8,000 to 10,000 square feet of drywall, and wallboard makers pass gas-price swings through within a quarter or two.
WPU137.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Nonmetallic Mineral Products: Gypsum Products

WPU0721.name: Plastic construction products
WPU0721.read: Producer price index for plastic pipe, siding, flooring and foam board. Tracks resin prices, which follow oil and natural gas.
WPU0721.example: For example: PVC drain and supply pipe, vinyl siding and foam sheathing all reprice with resin, so an oil or gas spike reaches the house through plastics as well as fuel.
WPU0721.title: Producer Price Index by Commodity: Rubber and Plastic Products: Plastic Construction Products

SPREAD.name: Mortgage spread over 10Y
SPREAD.read: Historically near 170bp and far wider since 2022. Compression improves affordability with no Fed move at all.

brief.headline: All nine builders reporting the summer quarter describe weaker demand. Horton's cancellation rate reached 23%, and impairments have reached California product.
national: Nine builders have now reported the summer quarter: Lennar and KB Home for quarters ended August 31, and D.R. Horton, PulteGroup, M/I Homes, Meritage, Century Communities, NVR and LGI Homes for September 30. All nine describe it as weaker than the quarter before. Every one but LGI delivered fewer homes than a year earlier (Horton down 2%, Lennar down 3%, Pulte down 9%, KB down 19%, M/I down 2%, Meritage down 14%, Century down 2%, NVR down 7%); LGI's closings rose 12% only because wholesale sales to rental operators climbed to 215 homes, 18% of the total. Net orders fell everywhere they are reported (Horton down 7%, Lennar down 9%, Pulte down 6%, KB down 12%, M/I down 2%, Meritage down 15%, Century down 4%, NVR down 7%), and LGI's are down 30% for the year to date. Margins are still compressed year over year: Horton's home sales margin was 20.2% for fiscal 2026 against 21.5% and about 19.5% in the September quarter, Lennar 15.8% against 17.5%, Pulte 24.8% against 26.2%, KB 16.5% against 18.2%, M/I homebuilding 18.4% against 21.5%, Meritage 17.4% against 19.1%, Century 15.0% against 17.9%, NVR 18.3% against 21.1%, LGI 20.2% against 21.5%. Lennar and KB did improve on their second quarters.

Rates are the stated cause. Lennar puts the 30-year mortgage at about 7% and the 10-year Treasury near 5%, up from 6.4% to 6.5% earlier in the year, and ties the move to energy-driven inflation from tension with Iran. M/I says mortgage rates topped 7% by quarter end, and Pulte says they rose sharply, most of all in September. Resale competition is building at the same time. KB says resale inventory is at its highest level in a decade with prices trending down in several of its markets, and Lennar reports rising resales in Texas and Florida. Meritage says buyers worried about the market and their own finances are in less of a hurry to commit, and Century reports that adjustable-rate loans were nearly 35% of its mortgage originations, up from under 5% in early 2025. Buyers are stretching for the payment.

Cancellations are where the third quarter breaks from the second. In the middle of the group, Pulte held at 16%, Lennar rose to 15% from 14%, KB to 18% from 17%, Meritage to 13% from 11%, and M/I sat at 12.3% against 12.2%; Century does not disclose a rate. Horton's rose to 23% in its September quarter from 20% a year earlier, and 19% for the fiscal year against 18%. NVR's rate rose to 21.0% from 19.4%, and LGI's reached 48.9% for the first nine months against 28.1% a year earlier, which LGI attributes to more buyers being unable to secure or keep mortgage financing. Its backlog fell 48% to 685 homes. Toll's 2.6% from the July quarter is still the other end of the gradient.

Incentives are now pulling in two directions. Lennar's fell again, to 12.0% of revenue from 14.3% a year earlier and 12.9% in its prior quarter, although its West segment went the other way. M/I's incentives and closing costs rose to $73.2 million from $53.5 million, with mortgage rate buydowns up $23.2 million, Pulte expects its incentives to stay elevated, Meritage expects to need higher incentive use, and Century's average delivered price fell 10% on incentives alone. Nobody is building into it. Pulte's unsold homes in production fell to 6,627 from 7,369 and its completed specs to 1,696 from 2,027. KB delivered 74% built-to-order and posted its first year-over-year backlog increase in four years. Lennar guides fourth-quarter orders of 19,500 to 20,500 against deliveries of 22,000 to 23,000, converting inventory to cash. Horton ended September with 17,700 unsold homes, 8,800 of them finished, expects incentives to stay elevated through fiscal 2027, and guides 79,000 to 84,000 closings for that year against 84,202 in fiscal 2026.
land: The new development in the third-quarter filings is builders using the option to exit. KB abandoned 8,777 previously controlled lots in its first nine months; its lots owned or controlled fell 5% to 61,581 since November, and the share held under option fell to 40% from 43%. Pulte says it has walked away from a number of land option agreements and is re-underwriting options before buying more land. Its controlled lots fell to 224,275 from 234,632 at year end, with 55% optioned against 57%, and its third-quarter land-related charges rose to $37.5 million from $27.6 million. Meritage has not finished evaluating, or committed to, 18,025 of the 36,644 lots it holds under purchase and option contracts, and it recovered deposits in the September quarter on deals it had already terminated. NVR, which buys finished lots rather than land, controls about 176,000 lots under purchase agreements backed by about $1.03 billion of deposits, and it wrote off $24.8 million of those deposits in the quarter against $18.9 million a year earlier.

Lennar stays at the land-light extreme: 11,808 homesites owned against 476,153 controlled, 98% of the total, and the total is down from more than 511,000 a year ago. About 86% of its third-quarter deliveries came through land banking. The cost of that model is now visible. Lennar says land cost per home has risen, partly through option maintenance fees on extended deal durations, and expects that to weigh on margin while it works through positions underwritten under earlier market conditions. M/I controls about 48,900 lots, roughly five years of supply and 3% fewer than a year ago, with 25,509 of them under option at an aggregate $1.74 billion. Century moved the other way on mix: of 60,969 lots, 54.9% are owned against 57.1% at year end, with controlled lots up 5.3%. LGI is the opposite model and the most exposed: it owns 50,270 of its 58,400 lots, while its backlog has halved.

Horton is shifting the same way. Its owned lots fell to 130,500 from 147,000 while optioned lots held at 440,100, so 77% of its 570,600 lots are now under purchase contracts against 75% a year earlier. Those contracts carry a remaining purchase price of $28.7 billion on $2.6 billion of deposits. 68% of fiscal 2026 closings were on lots developed by Forestar or third parties, up from 65%. Forestar itself is shrinking its book: 84,400 lots owned or controlled against 99,800, 13,545 lots sold in fiscal 2026, down 5%, and guidance of 12,000 to 13,000 lots for fiscal 2027.

They are still buying selectively. KB put $722.3 million into land in the quarter, up 40% from a year earlier, and ended with 277 communities, up 5%. Meritage bought about 6,500 lots for $410.9 million and spent $601.4 million on development in nine months, ending with 348 communities against 334. Century bought HistoryMaker Homes in Dallas on October 7 for about $160.2 million, adding 29 communities, and ended the quarter at 343 against 321. Pulte's average community count rose 7%, and M/I expects to finish the year about 5% higher. Toll held 75,500 lots with 58% under option at the end of its July quarter.

The land pricing note has turned more cautious. Pulte's second-quarter 10-Q said land inflation was easing. Its third-quarter 10-Q says instead that it continues to face pressure in the cost of land acquisition and development, and KB, M/I, Lennar and Meritage all name higher land or lot costs as a margin drag; Meritage says land costs remain elevated after years of high acquisition and development costs. NVR goes further and says it expects more margin pressure from higher land prices. None of the nine filings reports falling land prices.
socal: The third-quarter filings do speak to California, through each builder's western segment, and the read splits by builder.

Horton's Southwest region, which includes California, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Hawaii, lost the most ground on buyer commitment. Its fiscal 2026 cancellation rate rose to 19% from 15%, the largest increase of Horton's six regions, and closings fell 5% to 9,013, which Horton attributes particularly to Las Vegas and Southern California. Orders slipped 2% to 9,096 at an average $482,400, backlog rose 8% to 1,118 homes, and pre-tax margin held at 11.0% against 11.3%. The region controls 48,500 lots, 17,300 of them owned.

Lennar's West segment, which includes California, is its weakest. Gross margin was 12.1% against 16.3% a year earlier, the lowest of its four segments, and the filing cites lower average prices in California among other states from base price cuts and more incentives. West deliveries fell 8% to 4,529 and orders 9% to 4,319. It is also the one Lennar segment where incentives rose, to 10.9% of revenue from 10.5%.

Pulte's West segment, which also includes California, had closings down 18%, orders down 15% and a 21% cancellation rate, the highest of its six segments, and pre-tax income fell 57%. Average price rose 2% only because of closing mix in its California markets. West is where Pulte owns most of its land: 25,681 lots owned against 12,447 optioned, the reverse of its company-wide split.

KB's West Coast segment (California, Idaho and Washington) is the exception. Net orders rose 8% to 937, backlog value rose 22% to $1.02 billion, average community count rose 25% to 111, and the cancellation rate improved to 16% from 18%. Prices are giving: average selling price fell 6% to $641,800 and segment gross margin slipped to 16.7%. KB carries 20,471 West Coast lots at $3.21 billion, its largest land position by value. M/I and NVR have no California operations. LGI's West segment, which includes California, closed 239 homes against 203 at about $454,000 each, but the filing gives no West orders figure.

Century's West segment is California and Washington, and it is where the first real write-down landed. It lost $13.5 million before tax in the quarter, against a $21.2 million profit a year earlier, after $19.1 million of impairment charges. Deliveries fell 25%, orders 20.5% to 268, and average price 6.8% to $550,700 on heavier incentives. Century holds 3,562 owned and 2,309 controlled lots there.

Meritage's West region, which includes California, closed 20% fewer homes and took 19% fewer orders, with its sales pace down to 2.6 a month per community from 3.4 and cancellations up to 12% from 9%. Its West margin held up better than the company's at 18.0%.

One structural change: Sumitomo Forestry completed its acquisition of Tri Pointe on May 14, 2026 at $47 per share, delisting the company and making the group roughly the fifth largest U.S. builder at about 15,000 units annually. Tri Pointe reports Homebuilding Southern California as a named segment, so one of the most active regional counterparties is now a private subsidiary of a Japanese parent. Expect a different capital posture and no more quarterly segment disclosure.
ventura: No public builder discloses at county level. Ventura appears in none of these filings. Anything county-specific attributed to a builder filing is extrapolation.

The resale side, from Redfin's October county data in the resale panel on this board: median sale price $862,100, up 0.5% from a year earlier, on 509 sales, down 12.7%, with a 52-day median time on market and sales at 98.2% of list.
KB Home is actively selling at Beltramo Ranch in the county, and the new-home pipeline countywide is thin for a county of this size.

The two items that belong on the radar are regulatory, not corporate. The 2025 California Building Standards Code and local County amendments took effect for all applications submitted on or after January 1, 2026, and AB 1308 now requires the County to inspect completed residential work of one to ten units within ten business days, with a miss treated as a Housing Accountability Act violation. That second one is real leverage on close-out timing.
takeaway: Nine summer-quarter filings, all pointing weaker, strengthen the case against entitling entry-level detached product for a near-term sale. Finished lots in attainable price ranges are still the gap, but builders will now pay for them only on option terms they can walk away from.

Expect re-trades and walk-aways on options underwritten in 2024 and 2025. KB's 8,777 abandoned lots and Pulte's walk-aways are the evidence, and Lennar's rising option fees show the land bankers are pricing the extensions. For a land seller, deposit and extension terms now matter as much as headline price.

In California, KB's West Coast segment is the one builder book adding communities and orders, while Century's $19.1 million impairment is the first write-down in this group aimed at California and Washington product. Watch whether others follow in fourth-quarter filings. Horton names Southern California as a drag on its Southwest closings, where cancellations rose to 19% from 15%. Buyer financing is the new stress point: Horton's 23%, NVR's 21% and LGI's 49% cancellation rates mean anyone holding a PSA with an entry-level builder should expect slower takedowns. Toll's annual report for the year ended October 31, due in December, is the next read.

narrative.headline: D.R. Horton's CEO says the builder is not betting on lower mortgage rates in 2027 as it trims starts.

national: Nine builders have now reported the summer quarter: Lennar and KB Home for quarters ended August 31, and D.R. Horton, PulteGroup, M/I Homes, Meritage, Century Communities, NVR and LGI Homes for September 30. All nine describe it as weaker than the quarter before. Net orders fell everywhere they are reported (Horton down 7%, Lennar down 9%, Pulte down 6%, KB down 12%, M/I down 2%, Meritage down 15%, Century down 4%, NVR down 7%). LGI's third-quarter orders fell 61.2% to 609 homes, its management said on Nov 3, and it narrowed 2026 closings guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes on slower sales as affordability weighed [155][8].

M/I's CEO said the 10-year rose from 4.5% to 5.3% and mortgage rates from about 6.75% to 7.75% in the quarter, and M/I's September orders fell 16% [164]. Century's management said on Oct 28 that it cut 2026 deliveries to 9,350 to 9,650 homes and starts 8%, confirming the Nov 23 headline [73][159][67]. On Sep 16, Lennar cut full-year deliveries to 80,000 to 81,000 from 82,000 to 83,000 and guided fourth-quarter orders of 19,500 to 20,500 against deliveries of 22,000 to 23,000 [166].

Horton cut starts 10% [67]. It guides 79,000 to 84,000 closings for fiscal 2027 against 84,202 and expects elevated incentives, its management said Oct 29 [177]. On Nov 25, ResiClub reported that Horton's CEO is not betting on lower mortgage rates in 2027 [213]. Lance Lambert wrote on Nov 24 that Horton is cutting starts as unsold inventory climbs above pre-pandemic levels [219]. The 30-year fixed rate was 7.28% on Nov 19 and the 10-year 4.92% on both Nov 20 and Nov 23 [63][199], not the 5.04% quoted in earlier editions. HousingWire says sub-7% mortgages need a 10-year yield below 4.85% and 2% mortgage spreads [59].

Margins are still compressed year over year: Horton 20.2% against 21.5%, Lennar 15.8% against 17.5% and Meritage 17.4% against 19.1%, whose management expects 2022 to 2025 lot costs to weigh through at least 2027 [179]. Cancellations rose at the entry level: Horton's reached 23% from 20% [177], NVR's 21.0% from 19.4%, LGI's 53.8% from 33.6% [155]. Forestar guided on Oct 29 to 12,000 to 13,000 lots in fiscal 2027 against 13,545, and its average lot price fell to $108,300 from $115,700 [178]. Input costs remain high: materials PPI up 12.1% in October [65], steel futures up 52.4% and diesel 73.0% year to date on Nov 25 [212], yet Lennar's cost per square foot fell 6% [166] and Century's direct costs fell 2% [159]. Toll Brothers reports its year to Oct 31 in December.
west: Horton's Southwest region (California, Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico, Hawaii) lost the most ground on buyer commitment. Its fiscal 2026 cancellation rate rose to 19% from 15%, and closings fell 5% to 9,013, which Horton attributes particularly to Las Vegas and Southern California. Lennar's West segment gross margin was 12.1% against 16.3%, the lowest of its four segments. Pulte's West segment had orders down 15% and a 21% cancellation rate. On Nov 23, the Orange County Register reported Southern California home sales at a 21-year low [77], and The Cool Down reported California sales at a nearly 3-year low with the median price at $886,760 [129].

KB's West Coast segment looks like the exception: net orders rose 8% to 937, though average selling price fell 6% to $641,800. But KB's management said on Sep 22 that Southern California drove a roughly $20,000 cut to its fourth-quarter price outlook [165]. LGI's management said Nov 3 that Southern California is among its top markets at 3.4 closings per community per month [155]. Century's West segment lost $13.5 million before tax after $19.1 million of impairments, some in the Bay Area [159]. Meritage's management said Oct 28 it prioritizes margin over volume in California, which needs higher incentives, and its West orders fell to 706 from 867 [179].

Land sellers are holding out. Five Point's management said Oct 22 it will likely defer some 2026 land sales rather than sell in a weaker market, and revised full-year net income guidance to about $20 million [163]. Millrose's management said Oct 27 it had no option terminations and provided $1.1 billion for Dream Finders' Beazer deal [160]. Tri Pointe, now under Sumitomo Forestry, no longer discloses segments. KB's Albert Praw retires Nov 30 and will advise on land [5]. CBIA backed Prop. 45 to shorten CEQA review in posts through Nov 1 [173][175]. Yahoo reported Nov 24 that developers are eyeing Southern California golf courses for housing, and neighbors are angry [222].
ventura: No public builder discloses at county level. Ventura appears in none of these filings. Anything county-specific attributed to a builder filing is extrapolation. KB Home is actively selling at Beltramo Ranch in the county, and the new-home pipeline countywide is thin for a county of this size. City Ventures, a private builder, held a grand opening for Walnut Park in Simi Valley on Nov 14 [42]. The Ventura County Star reported on Nov 18 that Simi Valley annexed 302 acres with plans for a large development [153]. The reporting seen here gives no unit count or builder, so timing and entitlement path are unknown.

The resale side, from Redfin's October county data in the resale panel on this board: median sale price $862,100, up 0.5% from a year earlier, on 509 sales, down 12.7%, with a 52-day median time on market and sales at 98.2% of list. The Ventura County Star also reported on Nov 18 that county home prices dipped to a two-year low in October [168]. The headline gives no figure, so it cannot be reconciled with Redfin's 0.5% gain. The county's drop in sales fits the regional slump [77]. Next door, the Los Angeles Case-Shiller index was up 1.0% year over year in September, slowing from 1.4% in August [209].

The items that belong on the radar are regulatory, not corporate. The 2025 California Building Standards Code and local County amendments took effect for all applications submitted on or after January 1, 2026, and AB 1308 now requires the County to inspect completed residential work of one to ten units within ten business days, with a miss treated as a Housing Accountability Act violation. That second one is real leverage on close-out timing. A third item surfaced Nov 23: Ventura Planning supported employee housing code and zoning changes [85][87]. On Nov 19, a school district was reported weighing 130 apartments on the Janss site in Thousand Oaks [151].

calls.name: LGI Homes
calls.headline: Management said affordability and higher rates cut orders 61%, but margins, costs and balance sheet improved; closings guidance narrowed to 4,600 to 4,800.
calls.west: Management named Southern California among its top markets at 3.4 closings per community per month. The West segment had 239 closings, a $454 thousand average price and 29 communities. The CEO said quite a few new openings are planned in California.

points.text: Management reported Q3 net orders of 609 homes, down 61.2% year over year, with cancellations at 53.8% versus 33.6%. Backlog ended at 685 homes worth $273.7 million.

Management said higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability weighed on orders, and a rate spike over the last 60 days made buydowns costlier. Buyers still inquire, but fewer qualify and many need time.

Management said it is leaning into incentives like closing cost help, buydowns and forward rate commitments, community by community, but will not give up margin just to chase volume. Average price was $368 thousand.
Management reported homebuilding gross margin of 20.2% and adjusted margin of 23.7%, both up 40 basis points sequentially. SG&A fell to 14% of revenue, a 180 basis point improvement.

Management reported owned lots fell for a sixth quarter to 50.3 thousand, while controlled lots rose 18.1% to 8.13 thousand, 58.4 thousand in total. Inventory dollars fell $160 million, with no impairments.
Management reported net debt to capital of 40.6%, down 420 basis points year over year. Revolver commitments were extended to October 2030, and liquidity was $447.7 million.
Management narrowed 2026 closings guidance to 4,600 to 4,800 homes, reaffirmed other targets, and expects Q4 gross margin similar to Q3. The CEO expects over 180 communities by end of 2027.

calls.name: D.R. Horton
calls.headline: Higher mortgage rates and affordability limits pressured demand, and management expects elevated incentives through fiscal 2027.

points.text: Management said rising mortgage rates, affordability constraints and cautious consumer sentiment continued to pressure new home demand, making housing conditions more challenging during the fourth quarter.
Reported results: fourth quarter net orders fell 7% to 18,619 homes and 9% in value to $6.6 billion. The cancellation rate rose to 23% from 20%.

Management said operators adjusted incentives, pricing and starts community by community to align inventory with demand. The company expects incentives to remain elevated in fiscal 2027, depending on market conditions.
Reported results: fourth quarter pre-tax margin was 10.8% (homebuilding 10.6%), and net income fell 18% to $741.8 million, including $91.4 million of rental segment inventory impairments.
Reported results: 68% of fiscal 2026 closings were on lots from Forestar or third parties, up from 65%. Owned and controlled lots totaled 570,600, with 77% controlled through contracts.
Management cited strong liquidity ($7.2 billion) and low leverage (20.8% debt to capital). It repurchased $3.6 billion of stock in fiscal 2026 and raised the quarterly dividend 11% to $0.50.

Expectations: initial fiscal 2027 guidance calls for revenues of $30.0 billion to $32.0 billion, 79,000 to 84,000 homes closed, about $3.5 billion of operating cash flow and about $3.0 billion of buybacks.

calls.name: Forestar Group
calls.headline: Demand is pressured by affordability and rising mortgage rates, but management cites a strong balance sheet and $2.2 billion of contracted revenue.

points.text: Management said new home demand remains weighed down by affordability constraints and cautious consumer sentiment. Quarterly lots sold still rose 2% to 5,004, though revenue fell 13% to $580.8 million.
Management said rising mortgage rates added further pressure on demand in the fourth quarter, on top of the existing affordability constraints.
Management said it will balance the pace and price of lot sales with investment timing. Reported average price per lot was $108,300 in the quarter, down from $115,700 a year earlier.
Reported fourth quarter pre-tax income fell 31% to $78.6 million, with a 13.5% pre-tax margin. Results included a $10.0 million asset sale gain and $7.6 million of real estate impairments.
Forestar owned and controlled 84,400 lots, down from 99,800. Of 58,200 owned lots, 8,100 were fully developed and 21,500 were under contract, representing about $2.2 billion of future revenue.
Management highlighted $1.3 billion of liquidity, including $657.0 million of cash, a 6.7% net debt to capital ratio, and no senior note maturities until fiscal 2028.
For fiscal 2027, the company expects to deliver 12,000 to 13,000 lots and $1.4 billion to $1.5 billion of revenue, below fiscal 2026's 13,545 lots and $1.6 billion.

calls.name: Century Communities
calls.headline: Management said a sharp rise in mortgage rates hurt orders, deliveries and margins, so it cut full year guidance and expects higher incentives in Q4.
calls.west: Management did not give a California-specific view. Impairments covered six underperforming communities, including some in the Bay Area. West orders fell 20.5% to 268 and deliveries fell 24.7% to 278. Management saw the rate-driven incentive increase as consistent across regions.

points.text: Management said buyers grew cautious as rates rose about 75 basis points, slowing traffic and conversions. Net orders were 2,284, cancellations stayed low at 14.6%, and the weak trend continued into October.

Management said Q3 incentives averaged about 1,300 basis points versus 1,200 in Q2. It expects Q4 closings to carry incentives 200 to 250 basis points higher, split roughly 60% price and 40% mortgage.

Adjusted gross margin was 19.3%, down 70 basis points sequentially on incentives. GAAP margin was 15.0% after $19.6 million of impairments. Direct costs fell 2% and lot costs 3%; management expects direct cost savings to level off.

Management said affordability keeps weakening and rate volatility matters as much as the level. ARMs were nearly 35% of originations, and management sees them as a partial fix. Rates easing slightly gave only early, uncertain optimism.

Century held just over 60,000 owned and controlled lots, with owned down 8% and controlled up 7%. Options of over 27,000 lots are secured by $85 million of deposits. Starts were cut 8% year over year to 2,502.
Management now expects 2026 deliveries of 9,350 to 9,650 homes and home sales revenue of $3.3 billion to $3.4 billion, including about 100 HistoryMaker deliveries. It expects Q4 SG&A near 14%.

Management said it will prioritize liquidity and keep debt-to-capital at or below the current 36.8%. It repurchased $12 million of stock in Q3, bought HistoryMaker using a revolver now sized at $1.2 billion, and expects to pay down debt.

calls.west: Management said it prioritizes margin over volume in California, Denver and Arizona, which remain highly competitive and need higher incentives to move homes. West orders were 706 versus 867, though some affordable core infill West communities are doing well.

points.text: Orders were 3,083, down 15%, with absorption of 3.0 per month and a 13% cancellation rate. Management said affordability and job worries make buyers hesitate, though long-term demographic demand is unchanged.

Management said mortgage rates rose from about 6.6% to 7.5% during the quarter and the pressure continued into October. Without meaningful rate relief, it expects incentives to stay elevated near term.

calls.name: Millrose Properties
calls.headline: Management said the core business is performing strongly with no customer walking away, and raised fourth quarter AFFO guidance to $0.82 to $0.84.

points.text: Management said builders are showing renewed interest in reloading land after weaker same-store purchases as of June 30, and the CEO believes industry margins have largely troughed despite the recent rate spike.

Reported: Millrose funded about $1.3 billion of land and development, received about $800 million in homesite takedown proceeds, and had no option terminations. It held 156,729 homesites across 834 communities with 22 counterparties.

Management said it provided $1.1 billion for Dream Finders' Beazer deal: about $580 million land banking on 7,000 homesites and $488 million of 12% preferred. About 42% of assets now sit outside Lennar.

Debt to capital was 36% at quarter end. Management said it is comfortable temporarily exceeding 33%, will use takedown proceeds to pay debt back down, and authorized a $250 million buyback funded without borrowing.
Expectation: management raised its fourth quarter AFFO outlook to $0.82 to $0.84 per share, from $0.80 reported in Q3. Most of the lift is Dream Finders, and rental home carrying costs are included.

Management said 10-year rates above 5% pressure affordability, with over 30% of prospective buyers denied mortgages. Higher SOFR lifted other-agreement yields to 10.8%; management expects about 11% next quarter.

Management said the rental pilot bought 1,233 homes for about $333 million, with $120 million net equity. Roughly 10% are leased at rents about 10% above underwriting; further investment is paused pending evaluation.

calls.name: PulteGroup
calls.headline: Management said rising mortgage rates and inflation are pressuring demand, but a move-up and active-adult mix kept gross margin at 24.8%.

points.text: Management said homebuying demand is increasingly pressured by rising rates, inflation and global unrest. Net new orders were 6,208 homes, down 6%, with a value of $3.5 billion versus $3.6 billion.
The CEO said the rapid rise in interest rates stretched affordability further, made selling an existing home harder, and pushed more consumers to the sidelines.
Management said it is balancing price and pace of sales and aligning production to match. Average closing price was $561,000, down 1%. The release gave no incentive figures.

Home sale gross margin was 24.8% versus 26.2%, including about 70 basis points of land impairments. Management credited a mix of over 60% move-up and active-adult buyers. SG&A was 10.3% of revenue versus 9.4%.

Management said it stays disciplined on capital allocation. It repurchased $350 million of shares in the quarter and $1.0 billion over nine months, ending with $1.4 billion of cash and 12% debt-to-capital.
Management gave no West commentary. Reported West data show closings of 1,118 versus 1,359, orders of 945 versus 1,110, and backlog of 1,578 homes versus 1,814. California is not broken out.
The release gave no forward guidance, lot counts or land spend figures. Reported backlog rose 4% to 10,298 homes ($6.4 billion), and average community count rose 7% to 1,077.

calls.name: NVR
calls.headline: Management said gross margin fell to 18.3% on higher lot costs, pricing pressure from affordability challenges and weak consumer sentiment.

points.text: New orders fell 7% to 4,391 units and the cancellation rate rose to 21% from 19%. Backlog still grew 10% in units to 10,121 and 4% in dollars to $4.59 billion.
Management cited pricing pressure from continued affordability challenges and weak consumer sentiment. Average order price fell 5% to $442,100 and average settlement price fell 2% to $445,900.
Gross margin dropped to 18.3% from 21.0%. Management pointed to higher lot costs, pricing pressure and about $24.8 million of contract land deposit impairments. Net income fell 27% to $248.6 million.

Lots controlled rose to 185,300 from 175,300 a year earlier. Net contract land deposits were $916.7 million at quarter end, up from $851.5 million at December 31, 2025. No land spend figure was given.
NVR repurchased 37,088 shares for $237.2 million in the quarter and $1.23 billion over nine months. Homebuilding cash fell to $1.09 billion from $1.88 billion at year end.
The release gave no guidance or outlook, and no incentive or cycle time figures. It made no specific comments on interest rates beyond listing rate changes as a general risk factor.

calls.name: Five Point Holdings
calls.headline: Weak housing demand leads Five Point to likely defer 2026 land sales and revise full-year net income guidance to about $20 million.
calls.west: Management said it renewed the Great Park development management agreement through December 2028, secured entitlement approvals at Valencia for Homestead South, and broke ground at Candlestick in San Francisco. It remains confident in the long-term value of its California communities.

points.text: Management said current housing market conditions have hurt homebuyer demand. Builders sold 54 homes at Great Park and 92 homes at Valencia during the quarter.
Management said it will likely defer some land sales it had expected to close in 2026 rather than sell in a weaker market. Consolidated land sales revenue was zero in the quarter.
Management revised full-year 2026 guidance to roughly $20 million of consolidated net income. It said this reflects land sale timing, not a change in its view of land value.

Reported revenue was $14.6 million, mostly management fees from Great Park and Hearthstone. Selling, general and administrative expense was $12.5 million, and the consolidated net loss was $4.4 million.

Cash was $358.7 million and liquidity was $576.2 million, including an undrawn $217.5 million revolver. Debt to total capitalization was 16.2%. Management said this gives flexibility to be patient on land sales.

Great Park Venture distributions and incentive compensation payments to the company totaled $40.4 million in the quarter. Management also pointed to growing recurring fee revenue from Hearthstone and the Great Park.

calls.name: M/I Homes
calls.headline: Management said sharply higher rates hurt September demand and margins, but its land position and record balance sheet leave it well placed for a tougher market.

points.text: Management reported orders of about 1,860 homes, down 2%, with July up 15%, August down 6% and September down 16%. Cancellations were 12%. Half of sales went to first-time buyers.
The CEO said the 10-year Treasury rose from 4.5% to 5.3% and mortgage rates from about 6.75% to 7.75% in the quarter, hurting confidence. Rates have eased slightly, but choppy conditions may last.

Gross margin was 21.3% excluding $5 million of charges, down 23 basis points on costlier rate buydowns and higher lot costs. Management said incentives rose through the quarter. SG&A was 13.1% of revenue versus 11.9%.

Management said construction costs and cycle times were flat versus the second quarter. It sees more price cuts in some markets and more buyers choosing adjustable rate mortgages. Florida's Gulf Coast remains challenged.
Management said it owns about 23,400 lots (2.5 years) and controls 25,600 more by option, roughly 49,000 total. It spent $290 million on land in the quarter and will be more careful on new deals.

Management cited record equity of $3.3 billion, $620 million cash, no borrowings on the $900 million revolver and net debt to capital of 2%. It spent $50 million on buybacks, with $200 million authorized.

Management gave no numeric guidance. It expects year-end community count about 5% higher, has trimmed starts, plans no major strategy change, and will control hiring and expenses. It said demand, not land or labor, is the constraint.

calls.name: KB Home
calls.headline: Weaker demand and higher rates cut the Q4 price and margin outlook, driven by Southern California, while full-year delivery guidance holds.
calls.west: Management said Southern California caused the Q4 outlook cut. Slower third quarter sales reduced closings of higher-priced homes, the mix of communities delivering shifted, and some high-ASP openings were missed. points.text: Management said conditions weakened since June. Traffic was down about 10% year over year, sales softened in July and August, and net orders fell year over year as cautious buyers waited.

Management said rising mortgage rates and a Fed hike hurt affordability, and rates rose another 20 to 30 basis points since August. Faster 99 day builds make early rate locks easier, so incentive adjustments stay minimal.

Reported adjusted housing gross margin was 16.8% versus 18.9% a year ago, up from 15.7% in Q2, helped by a 74% Built to Order mix. Management expects slightly higher Q4 direct costs from fuel and tariffs.

Management expects Q4 deliveries of 3,000 to 3,500, housing revenue of $1.45 billion to $1.65 billion, ASP near $480,000 (prior view $500,000), and gross margin of 16% to 16.6%. Full-year gross margin is guided to 16% to 16.2%.

Management said Southern California drove the roughly $20,000 Q4 ASP cut through slower sales, community mix and missed openings, and competitive pricing pressured its margins. Northern California is performing as expected.

Management cited over 61,000 lots owned or controlled and nearly $725 million of land spend, with the increase mostly development and fees. The executive chairman expects land spend to come down a little.
Management repurchased about 890,000 shares and plans up to $50 million more in Q4. Debt-to-capital was 35.7%, liquidity was $942 million, and the long-term 22% gross margin target stays.

calls.name: Lennar
calls.headline: Management said conditions worsened as rates rose and confidence fell, so it held volume with heavy incentives and lowered its full-year delivery target.

points.text: Management reported new orders down 9% to 20,879 homes and deliveries of 20,840, within guidance. Sales and start pace were both 4.1 homes per community per month across 1,713 communities.
Management said the 30-year mortgage rate was about 6.8% at quarter end and higher since, with inflation above the Fed target. It said weaker confidence and affordability are slowing buyer decisions.
Management said the $372,000 average sales price reflected about 12.0% incentives plus base price cuts needed to sustain volume, calling affordability the defining constraint.
Management reported gross margin of 15.8%, up sequentially, SG&A of 9.2% and net margin of 6.6%. Construction cost per square foot fell 6% year over year, and cycle time hit a record 116 days.
Management said it owns fewer than 2.5% of roughly 488,000 homesites owned and controlled. Completed unsold inventory fell to 1.8 homes per community from 2.1, and inventory turn is 2.4 times.
Management reported $1.2 billion in cash after repurchasing 3 million shares for $256 million and repaying $400 million of senior notes. Homebuilding debt to total capital was 16.6%.
Management expects Q4 orders of 19,500 to 20,500, deliveries of 22,000 to 23,000 and gross margin of 15.5% to 16.0%. It cut full-year deliveries to 80,000 to 81,000 from 82,000 to 83,000.

calls.name: Toll Brothers
calls.headline: Management called it a solid quarter in a challenging market, reaffirmed full-year guidance, and raised planned fiscal 2026 buybacks to $700 million.

points.text: Management called the market challenging but noted net signed contracts rose 5% year over year to 2,508 homes, or $2.52 billion. Cancellations fell to 5.4% of signed contracts from 7.5%.
Reported adjusted gross margin was 25.6%, 35 basis points above guidance but down from 27.5% a year ago. GAAP margin was 23.9%, and SG&A rose to 10.0% of revenue from 8.8%.
Management expects full-year home sales revenue of about $10.5 billion and a 26.1% adjusted gross margin. Fourth quarter guidance is 3,450 to 3,550 deliveries and a 26.0% adjusted margin.

Reported land spend was $451.9 million for about 2,784 lots. Lots owned and optioned totaled about 75,500, 42% owned. Management expects 8% to 10% community count growth in fiscal 2026, with similar growth in 2027.

Management said it returned $231 million to stockholders in the quarter and $506 million year to date. It raised planned fiscal 2026 repurchases from $650 million to $700 million, citing low leverage and ample liquidity.

Management gave no Pacific commentary. The segment table, which includes California, Oregon and Washington, shows Q3 contracts of 271 homes versus 284, with a lower average contract price of $1.47 million versus $1.80 million, and backlog of 524 homes versus 753.
